A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Learning Continually by Spectral Regularization. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original continual-learning experiments, generalization results, sensitivity tests, and network diagnostics in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original supervised-learning results and adds tiny-ImageNet, class-incremental, and DMC reinforcement-learning experiments, including architectural and stability diagnostics.

M1.justification: The spectral penalty, k=2, single power iteration, and treatment of biases, normalization parameters, and convolutional layers remain unchanged. Wasserstein regularization remains evaluated but becomes a cited baseline. Applying the existing regularizer to SAC introduces no described revision to the regularization procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds tiny-ImageNet evaluations, growing-class scenarios, and seven DMC continuous-control environments. The earlier MNIST-family, SVHN2, CIFAR, and binary Continual ImageNet coverage remains; the latter is distinct from the newly added tiny-ImageNet experiments.

E2.justification: v2 adds streaming EWC and SAC comparisons against LayerNorm alone and LayerNorm plus resets. The corresponding ResNet random-label comparison adds CReLU and omits Wasserstein, while pixel-permutation comparisons add shrink-and-perturb and EWC. v1's separate AdamW, CReLU, and ReDO MNIST panels are removed.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes the reported CIFAR10/100 random-label horizon from 25 to 30 tasks. New protocols include class increments of five, tiny-ImageNet splits and training budgets, and SAC with 16 updates per environment step and replay-buffer comparisons of 1 million versus 250,000 transitions. These are substantial evaluation-design additions; the stated horizon revision alone does not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: v2 adds representation-change diagnostics, a ViT random-label memorization failure case, larger-image regularization-strength tests, and RL buffer-size, sensitivity, gradient-norm, and Q-overestimation analyses. Earlier epoch, nonstationarity, k, and single-task-capacity analyses largely remain. Separate MNIST baseline diagnostics and some condition-number/singular-value-spread displays disappear.

E5.justification: Appendix B changes the stated regularization-sweep seed count from five to four for retained image datasets. Both versions otherwise report ten seeds and standard-error shading; the added RL results use mean and standard-error reporting.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include tiny-ImageNet accuracy, the ViT memorization failure in Figure 9, and DMC returns. v2 Figure 5 shows competitive aggregate performance against resets with the 1-million buffer and higher returns with the 250,000 buffer. Newly included shrink-and-perturb results exceed spectral regularization's mean accuracy on ViT/CIFAR10 in Figure 2, qualifying its comparative standing.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1 Appendix A.1's formal equal-difficulty specification and Section 4.1/Appendix A.6's Wasserstein formulation and comparison inequality. The central Jacobian bounds, gradient-rank argument, spectral-growth reasoning, and illustrative derivations remain substantially unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion change from proposing two regularizers to presenting spectral regularization as the sole methodological contribution. They also extend the main applicability claim from continual supervised learning to reinforcement learning, specifically mitigation of primacy bias in SAC.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting representation change to capacity use and RL stability to overestimation and parameter/gradient norms. It introduces a ViT generalization-versus-memorization tradeoff and explains how class-incremental and RL tasks violate equal-difficulty assumptions. The earlier broadly negative account of shrink-and-perturb becomes a more setting-dependent interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds substantive reproduction information: tiny-ImageNet splits and budgets, two-layer 256-unit SAC actor/critic networks, a single critic, 10,000 initial random transitions, replay-buffer sizes, and a shared 1e-4 regularization coefficient. Conversely, the self-contained Wasserstein construction in v1 Section 4.1 and Appendix A.6 is removed.

R1.justification: Wasserstein regularization changes from a claimed new contribution to a baseline attributed to Lewandowski et al. (2023). Positioning expands to streaming forgetting mitigation and high-replay-ratio RL/reset research, with new references including D'Oro, Ball, and Nauman. The Dohare preprint-to-Nature update represents retained work, not an additional research contribution.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, method organization, experimental discussion, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around spectral regularization. Generalization becomes the opening comparison, sensitivity material moves into Appendix C.4, and RL takes the final experimental subsection. Author information, headings, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 substantially rebuilds the main figure sequence, adds tiny-ImageNet and RL panels, relocates sensitivity figures, and consolidates network-property plots into Figure 14. Legends, colors, panel arrangements, captions, and document styling change extensively. The earlier generalization caption incorrectly naming random labels is corrected to pixel permutations.

improvement.justification: The class-incremental and SAC/DMC experiments substantially strengthen evidence beyond v1's supervised image-classification setting. Streaming-EWC and reset controls make comparative claims more credible, while the ViT failure analysis clarifies an applicability boundary. Most earlier supporting analyses remain. These gains outweigh the loss of separate MNIST baseline panels and Wasserstein detail, although inconsistent regularization/normalization terminology in Section 5.4 remains a documentation weakness.
